newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian stock markets seen drifting during holiday.
newsitem.headline: Asian stock markets seen drifting during holiday.

text.p: Asian stock markets are expected to drift in the coming week, with trade thin in the Christmas holiday period.
Brokers said a resurgent Wall Street would buoy some bourses but scepticism in Tokyo over government economic policy would adversely affect stocks.
Hong Kong's key Hang Seng index would maintain its positive tone but analysts said the holidays would suppress activity.
Concern in Bangkok about non-performing loans would hit the banking sector, brokers said.
TOKYO - Tokyo stocks will likely fall further in the coming week on spreading scepticism about the government's handling of the economy, brokers said.
The key Nikkei share average broke a three-day losing streak on Friday, helped by an overnight spurt on Wall Street.
But brokers predicted that the rebound would be temporary.

"The Nikkei posted a mild recovery just because of the New York rally but I still expect it to head downwards next week or in January," Haruyoshi Mabuchi, chief strategist at Nikko Research Centre, said on Friday.
"I think it is very possible that the Nikkei will dip to 19,000 by the end of the year," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.
On Friday, the Nikkei 225 average closed at 19,690.46, down 650.93 points from the previous week.
HONG KONG - Hong Kong stocks are expected to retain a positive tone but trade in a narrow range on reduced activity in the Christmas holiday week ahead, analysts said.

The Hang Seng Index closed at 13,131.41 points on Friday, after posting its biggest point gain since August 1994, with a rise of 284.85 points. The index rose 2.71 percent last week for a total 30.36 percent gain this year.
"Hong Kong's performance is already very good so I don't see any need to window dress this year," said Franklin Lam, director of research at HG Asia.
BANGKOK - The Thai stock market is expected to remain sluggish on lack of buying from foreign investors on holiday.
"...people are off on holiday," said Sriyan Pietersz, the strategist at Capital Nomura Securities. "There'll be no trade and the market will be weak."
Brokers said the lingering concern about the asset quality of commercial banks may prompt a continuing offload of bank shares.
The SET index closed on Friday at 816.79 points from 872.67 a week ago.
BOMBAY - Indian shares are expected to extend a five-day rally to end 1996 on a hopeful note, dealers said.
"The market's winning streak has reversed the bearish mood," said a dealer at a local brokerage. "We expect a surge next week."
Most Indian bourses are open for only two days before closing for the Christmas holidays.
The benchmark 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange jumped 228.54 points or about 8 percent for the week to end at a provisional 3,110.19 over last Friday's close of 2,881.65.
DHAKA - Dhaka stocks suffered another bearish week, hit by downturns in high priced shares and investor caution.
Brokers also attributed the slide to fund shortages. With the year-end approaching, banks were reluctant to give loans despite the lifting of credit restrictions.
The DSE benchmark index lost 69.4 points to finish at 2,587.2 in the week ending Thursday.
JAKARTA - Brokers and analysts said the market was expected to be mixed in quiet trading, with many investors away for Christmas.
"Volume-wise, trading will be quieter. But the index could stay on the positive side on locally led speculative buying," an analyst with a local firm said.
On Friday, the Jakarta Composite Index closed at 632.52 points, against last week's close of 624.46 points.
KUALA LUMPUR - For the week, the Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks rose 14.61 points to end at 1,203.06.
Dealers expect the Christmas week to be quiet, with many participants out and foreign markets doing minimal business.
The market is closed on Wednesday for Christmas.
MANILA - Window-dressing by fund managers will continue to support the Philippine equities market, traders said.
"There will be an upward bias as portfolio rationalisation and window dressing will continue next week," said Jonas Ferrer, research director at Pryce Securities.
The main index closed higher this week, by 60.2 points, or 1.93 percent at 3,180.20, from 3,120 points last week.
SEOUL - Seoul shares are expected to remain strong early in the week due to buying by public pension funds and improved sentiment, brokers said.

"Because of the pension fund buying, we think the index has the potential to rise to around the 730-740 level," a Shinhan Securities broker said. Buying is likely to be focused on blue chips and large-cap, heavily weighted shares, they said.
On Friday, the composite index closed at 700.87, up 11.8 points, or 1.71 percent, from last Friday's closing of 689.07.
SINGAPORE - Dealers said they expected Singapore shares to remain steady in holiday-thinned trading.
"There is some window dressing going on by funds because of the year-end but volume should remain thin," said a broker with a local firm.
Dealers said Singapore stocks may also get support from funds which are switching out of the plunging Thai stockmarket.
The Straits Times Industrial index closed at 2,196.81 on Friday, up 17.65 points over the previous week.
SYDNEY - Australian shares looked strong in the near term with a resurgent Wall Street market leading the way.
The All Ordinaries index closed at 2,373.8 on Friday, up 57.3 points over the week.

Despite heading into the Christmas break, brokers said buyers showed few signs of quitting. Friday's session saw a one-day record of A$1.73 billion (US$1.38 billion) worth of shares traded and the index jumped 42.1 points.

TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are expected to rise to test the 7,000-point resistance level, on Thursday's news that local regulators had raised the stock investment ceiling for individual foreign funds, brokers said.
The ceiling was lifted to US$600 million from US$400 million.
"In a market that is entering consolidation, such news is a good indicator showing the government's position on the bullish side," said Amy Huang, an analyst at Nomura Securities.
On Friday, the index ended at 6,890.66 points, compared with 6,825.10 a week ago. A 6,850-7,050 range was seen for next week, brokers said.
WELLINGTON - New Zealand shares ended the week strongly after the market took heart from a resurgence in U.S. markets, but the market was little changed from its week-ago level.

"With the Dow up... it looks like their bull market is well and truly back in force, so should the offshore markets be strong I would expect New Zealand to rise throughout the holiday period," Tim Koller from Hendry Hay said.
The NZSE-40 Capital Index closed at 2,349.98, only fractionally changed from last week's close of 2,349.91.
